events.label: Congress passes the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act
events.desc: Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010 (S. 3307) enacted as Public Law 111-296. Among its provisions: direct certification performance targets (Sec. 101), a Medicaid direct certification demonstration (Sec. 103) and community eligibility (Sec. 104). Effective dates are set by section; the school-year dates in the later rows come from the text.

events.label: States get targets for direct certification: 80 percent at first, rising to 95
events.desc: Sets a 'required percentage' for direct certification: 80 percent for the school year beginning July 1, 2011, 90 percent for the school year beginning July 1, 2012, and 95 percent for the school year beginning July 1, 2013 and each school year thereafter. Each school year the Secretary identifies States that directly certify less than the required percentage of the children in the State who are eligible for direct certification, and requires those States to implement a continuous improvement plan.
events.cite: Pub. L. 111-296, Sec. 101; 124 Stat. 3186; Richard B. Russell National School Lunch Act Sec. 9(b)(4)(F)

events.label: Schools get an option to serve free meals to all students, with no meal forms
events.desc: Community eligibility created. An agency or school may elect special assistance payments in place of payments based on applications, over a 4-year period, serving all children free lunch and breakfast. 'Identified students' are students certified from documentation of benefit receipt or categorical eligibility under 7 CFR 245.6a(c)(2). For school years beginning on or before July 1, 2013, the threshold is 40 percent identified students and the multiplier is 1.6.
events.cite: Pub. L. 111-296, Sec. 104; 124 Stat. 3193 to 3195; Richard B. Russell National School Lunch Act Sec. 11(a)(1)(F)

events.label: The option starts in Illinois, Kentucky and Michigan, with 4 more added in each of the next two years
events.desc: Community eligibility phase-in: the Secretary may approve agencies and schools in 3 States for the school year beginning July 1, 2011, and in an additional 4 States for each of the school years beginning July 1, 2012 and July 1, 2013. The statute does not name the States. USDA's 2013 proposed rule (D056, 78 FR 65891) names them: Illinois, Kentucky and Michigan for the school year beginning July 1, 2011; Ohio, New York, District of Columbia and West Virginia for the school year beginning July 1, 2012; Florida, Georgia, Maryland and Massachusetts for the school year beginning July 1, 2013.

events.label: A trial begins: selected districts certify children for free meals through Medicaid, with no application
events.desc: Medicaid direct certification demonstration: selected local educational agencies certify eligible children for free meals without further application beginning the school year July 1, 2012. Scope: agencies serving 2.5 percent of students certified for free and reduced-price meals nationwide in 2012, 5 percent in 2013, and 10 percent in 2014 and each year after.

events.label: USDA proposes rules for the free-meals-for-all option
events.desc: USDA Food and Nutrition Service published a proposed rule to add community eligibility to 7 CFR 245 (new 245.9(f)): 4-year option, 40 percent minimum identified student percentage, 1.6 multiplier, no household applications at participating schools. Comments due January 3, 2014. Text says the provision becomes available nationally for the school year beginning July 1, 2014. The statute's regulation deadline was December 31, 2013.

events.label: The option opens to every eligible district in the country
events.desc: Community eligibility open to any eligible local educational agency for school years beginning on or after July 1, 2014. From that date the Secretary may use a threshold below 40 percent and a multiplier between 1.3 and 1.6, and may set different multipliers for different schools or agencies. The Secretary must issue regulations by December 31, 2013; a proposed rule followed on November 4, 2013 (US-D7) and the final rule on July 29, 2016 (US-D8).

events.label: Every Student Succeeds Act: report cards must show results for economically disadvantaged students
events.desc: Every Student Succeeds Act (Pub. L. 114-95), approved December 10, 2015. Sec. 1005 rewrites section 1111 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (20 U.S.C. 6311). Under 6311(h)(1)(C), each State report card must include student achievement on the State assessments for all students and disaggregated by each subgroup of students described in 6311(b)(2)(B)(xi) (clause (ii)), and high school graduation rates for all students and disaggregated by each of the subgroups of students defined in 6311(c)(2) (clause (iii)(II)). Both lists name economically disadvantaged students ((b)(2)(B)(xi)(II); (c)(2)(A)). The Act uses the term economically disadvantaged 10 times and does not define it or say how it is measured. Effective dates, Pub. L. 114-95 Sec. 5: the Act is effective upon enactment except as otherwise provided (5(a)); subsections (c) and (d) of section 1111 take effect beginning with school year 2017-2018 (5(e)(1)(B)); any other provision of section 1111 takes effect in a manner consistent with subsection (a) (5(e)(1)(C)).

events.label: USDA’s final rules for the option take effect
events.desc: USDA Food and Nutrition Service final rule adding community eligibility to 7 CFR 245: 4-year option or grace year, identified student percentage of at least 40 percent as of April 1 of the prior school year, free claiming percentage equal to the identified student percentage times 1.6, annual SNAP data match, election documentation to the State agency by June 30. Effective, and compliance begins, August 29, 2016.

events.label: A pandemic law lets USDA waive school meal rules nationwide
events.desc: Families First Coronavirus Response Act, Div. B (Nutrition Waivers), Title II (COVID-19 Child Nutrition Response Act), Sec. 2202, approved March 18, 2020. (a) The Secretary of Agriculture may establish a waiver for all States under section 12(l) of the National School Lunch Act for providing meals and meal supplements under a qualified program with appropriate safety measures with respect to COVID-19. (b) The Secretary may grant a waiver to allow non-congregate feeding under the child and adult care food program. (c) The Secretary may grant a waiver relating to the nutritional content of meals where there is a supply chain disruption due to COVID-19. Qualified programs are the school lunch, school breakfast, child and adult care food and summer food service programs. (e) In the original text the authority expires on September 30, 2020. The words free meal, free lunch and free breakfast do not appear in the Act.
events.cite: Pub. L. 116-127, Div. B, Title II, Sec. 2202

events.label: Keep Kids Fed Act sets end dates for the pandemic waivers and adds money per meal
events.desc: Keep Kids Fed Act of 2022, approved June 25, 2022. Sec. 2(a): each school lunch receives an additional 40 cents and each school breakfast an additional 15 cents, only for the school year beginning July 2022. Sec. 2(b) amends Families First Sec. 2202: authority for waivers under subsection (a) expires on September 30, 2022; after June 30, 2022 such a waiver applies only to schools or sites operating the summer food service program or the option in section 13(a)(8) of the National School Lunch Act and not operating the school lunch program; authority for the child and adult care food program waiver expires on June 30, 2022; authority for the meal pattern waiver expires on June 30, 2023. Sec. 2(d): for school year 2022-2023 the Secretary may establish waivers under section 12(l) on a nationwide basis without State applications; such a waiver shall not be in effect after June 30, 2023. The Act does not mention community eligibility or universal free meals by name.

events.desc: USDA Food and Nutrition Service final rule lowers the minimum identified student percentage for community eligibility from 40 percent to 25 percent. The multiplier stays at 1.6. The text read ties the threshold to April 1 of the school year before implementing CEP and does not name a first school year.
